children: STOCKS AFTER THE FIRST FED HIKE OF A CYCLE: SMALL DIP, BIG UNCERTAINTY
What effect is the Fed's freshly launched interest rate cycle likely to have on the U.S. stock market?
Perhaps some weakness over the next two months, but with a highly variable outcome 12 months down the road, limited data suggests.

Higher interest rates are generally bad news for stocks, as safe-bet Treasuries become relatively more attractive compared to riskier stocks, and as higher interest rates make it more costly for companies to borrow and operate their businesses.

However, stock market performance data since 1994, when the Federal Open Market Committee began announcing its rate target change on the day of its meeting, suggests that any negative effect from higher rates is hard to isolate from the many other factors moving markets at any given time.

Interest rate futures suggest Wednesday's 25 basis point increase is likely to be followed by more rate hikes, according to LSEG data, making this the start of a new cycle of tightening monetary policy.
Thursday's stock rally, with the S&P 500
surging over 1%, suggests that stock investors are willing to look beyond the negative aspects of higher interest rates.

The Fed has kicked off only six rate hike cycles since 1994, making for a small sample size to draw conclusions from. LSEG data analyzed by Reuters shows that the S&P 500 fell an average of 3.6% in the 60 calendar days after each of those six cycles began, usually down modestly, but once sharply up almost 8%.
By comparison, the S&P 500 gained an average of 1.6% over all two-month periods since 1994.

Looking longer term, the S&P 500 saw an average gain of 8.3% in the 12 months after the start of each rate hike cycle, with its performance varying from anywhere between a loss of 11% and a massive gain of 39% in those instances. That compares to a baseline average gain of about 10% over all 12-month periods, since 1994.

In other words, the Fed's first hike does appear to nudge stocks lower, at least briefly — but with only six cycles to compare and outcomes ranging so widely, it's just one of many inputs and not a signal investors should rely on.
